lessons.title: Every way to make it harder

blocks.markdown:
## Not just more weight

Progressive overload means asking a little more over time (Module 0). With home kit, adding weight is often the hardest option, because the next dumbbell can be a big jump. Luckily, there are many other dials.

blocks.alt: A ladder of ways to progress, from easiest to apply: more reps, more sets, slower lowering, pauses, more range, harder variation or leverage, one side at a time, less rest (density), more load.
blocks.caption: Ways to progress an exercise

blocks.markdown:
## The options

- **Reps:** one more rep per set.
- **Sets:** one more set (within your weekly volume).
- **Tempo:** a slower lowering phase, for example 3 seconds.
- **Pauses:** a 1–2 second stop at the hardest point.
- **Range:** deeper squats, deficit push-ups.
- **Variation:** a harder version, such as split squat to Bulgarian, or incline to floor push-ups.
- **One side at a time:** the same weight on one leg or arm.
- **Density:** the same work in less time.
- **Load:** the next weight up.

## Pick one at a time

Use one method per exercise per block, and track it. Reps first, then load, is the default (Lesson 2). The others come in when the next weight is too big a jump (Lesson 3).
**What this means for your training:** for each exercise, decide how it will progress this block: usually reps then load, otherwise tempo, pauses, range or a harder variation.

cards.back: More reps or sets, slower lowering, pauses, more range, harder variations, one side at a time, less rest.
Choose one progression method per exercise per block, so you can see what works.

questions.stem: Your heaviest dumbbell is 10 kg and split squats are getting easy. Which isn't a progression?
options: Doing the same 3 × 12 with the same weight and tempo
questions.explanation: Nothing changed, so there's no added demand.

blocks.markdown:
## Sources

1. **Guideline** — ACSM Position Stand, Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults, Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41(3):687–708.
2. **Practice** — programming conventions used in strength coaching; labelled as practice in the lesson.
3. **Image** — own diagram.

## Reps first, then weight

**Double progression** uses a rep range, for example 8–12, and two steps:

1. Keep the weight, and add reps session by session until every set reaches the top of the range with at least 1 rep in reserve.
2. Then increase the weight, and start again near the bottom of the range.

blocks.alt: A chart over eight sessions: reps per set climb from 8 to 12 at 10 kg, then the weight steps up to 12 kg and reps drop back to 8, then climb again.
blocks.caption: Double progression: reps, then weight

blocks.markdown:
## An example (illustrative)

One-arm row, 3 sets of 8–12 reps:

- Week 1, 12 kg: 10, 9, 8
- Week 2, 12 kg: 11, 10, 9
- Week 3, 12 kg: 12, 11, 10
- Week 4, 12 kg: 12, 12, 12, with 1–2 reps in reserve: move up
- Week 5, 16 kg: 8, 8, 7

## Wide ranges help with big jumps

If the jump to the next weight is large, use a wider range, like 10–15 or 12–20. You'll have more room to grow into the heavier weight. The load helper does the sums for you.

blocks.title: Load helper
blocks.description: Enter your rep range, the weight you used, the reps you did in each set and your available weights. It tells you whether to add reps, move up, or use another option because the jump is too big.

blocks.markdown: **What this means for your training:** give every main exercise a rep range and use double progression. Move up only when all sets hit the top of the range with a rep or two to spare.

cards.back: Add reps until all sets reach the top of the range with ≥1 rep in reserve; then add weight and start near the bottom.
Use a wider rep range (10–15 or 12–20) so the next weight is reachable.

questions.stem: Range 8–12. Last session at 10 kg: 12, 12, 11. What next?
options: Stay at 10 kg and aim for 12, 12, 12
Add a fourth set at 12 kg
questions.explanation: Not every set has reached the top yet.

lessons.title: When the next weight is too heavy

blocks.markdown:
## The gap problem

Going from 10 to 12.5 kg dumbbells is a 25% jump; from 12 to 16 kg kettlebells, 33%. That's often too much to keep the reps. Before buying more kit, use options that make the current weight harder.

blocks.alt: A gap between two weights, 12 kg and 16 kg, bridged by four steps: more reps beyond the range, slower lowering and pauses, one side at a time, then the heavier weight for fewer reps.
blocks.caption: Bridging a big weight jump

blocks.markdown:
## Tempo and pauses

A 2015 meta-analysis found that rep durations from about half a second to 8 seconds built similar muscle; very slow reps of more than about 10 seconds may be less effective. So a 3-second lowering or a 2-second pause is a useful tool, while super-slow reps are not.

## The bridging sequence

1. Extend the range: keep adding reps, up to about 20.
2. Slow the lowering to 3 seconds, or add a pause.
3. Switch to a one-sided or harder version.
4. Try the heavier weight for one set, then two, at the bottom of the range.
5. If none of these work, it's time for new kit (Module 3).
**What this means for your training:** when the next weight is too big a jump, add reps, slow the lowering, pause or go one-sided before you buy. Avoid super-slow reps of 10 seconds or more.

cards.back: Reps of about 0.5–8 seconds built similar muscle; super-slow reps (> ~10 s) may be less effective.
More reps → slower lowering or pauses → one-sided or harder version → heavier weight for one set, then two.

questions.stem: Which tempo change is least useful for muscle growth?
questions.explanation: Very slow reps beyond about 10 seconds appear less effective.

blocks.markdown:

2. **Practice** — programming conventions used in strength coaching; labelled as practice in the lesson.

## If it isn't written, it didn't happen

Progression needs a record. For each exercise, write the weight, the reps in each set and how many reps you had in reserve on the last set. A notes app, paper or a spreadsheet all work.

blocks.alt: A simple log table with columns: date, exercise, weight, reps per set, RIR on last set, note. Example rows for goblet squat and one-arm row over two sessions, with progress highlighted.
blocks.caption: A one-minute training log

blocks.markdown:
## The weekly review

Once a week, look across the log:

- Which exercises progressed?
- Which stalled for 2–3 sessions?
- How were sleep and energy?

Then set next week's targets. That's the 'adjust' step of the training loop (Module 0).

## Keep it light

One line per exercise is enough. Skip the stopwatch and the heart-rate charts. What matters is that next week's session can beat this one.
**What this means for your training:** log weight, reps and RIR for every exercise, every session, and review it once a week to set targets.

cards.back: Date, exercise, weight, reps per set, reps in reserve on the last set, a short note.
What progressed, what stalled for 2–3 sessions, how sleep and energy were; then set next week's targets.

questions.explanation: Weight, reps per set and effort make the next session plannable.

## Planned easy weeks

A **deload** is a period of reduced training stress, designed to reduce physical and mental fatigue, help recovery and prepare for the next block. That's the definition agreed by coaches in a 2023 international Delphi consensus.

blocks.alt: Bars for weekly training stress over ten weeks: four to six weeks rising gradually, one deload week at about half, then a new block starting slightly higher.
blocks.caption: Build, deload, build again

blocks.markdown:
## How to do it (practice)

- **When:** every 4–8 weeks, or sooner if warning signs appear.
- **How long:** about one week.
- **How:** keep the exercises and roughly the same weights, but do about half the sets, and stop further from failure (3–4 reps in reserve).
- **Sport:** keep it as normal, or ease off if matches are frequent.

## Warning signs

- Performance drops for two sessions in a row.
- Sleep is poor, or motivation has disappeared.
- Joints ache in a way that doesn't fade between sessions.

One bad day isn't a pattern; two or three are.
**What this means for your training:** plan a lighter week every 4–8 weeks: half the sets, same exercises, further from failure. Take it sooner if performance drops for two sessions in a row.

cards.back: A planned period of reduced training stress to shed fatigue and prepare for the next block (2023 Delphi consensus).
About one week; same exercises and weights; roughly half the sets; 3–4 reps in reserve.

questions.stem: Your log shows lower reps on two lifts for two sessions in a row, and you've slept badly. What's sensible?
questions.explanation: Two sessions of decline plus poor sleep are classic deload signs.

blocks.markdown:

1. **Consensus** — Bell L, Strafford BW, Coleman M, Androulakis Korakakis P, Nolan D, Integrating deloading into strength and physique sports training programmes: an international Delphi consensus approach, Sports Med Open 2023;9.
2. **Practice** — programming conventions used in strength coaching; labelled as practice in the lesson.

## When progress stops

A **plateau** is when a lift hasn't progressed for 2–3 weeks despite consistent training. Before changing the programme, check the usual suspects. Most plateaus aren't about the exercises.

blocks.alt: A checklist for a stalled lift: sets close to failure? Sleep 7+ hours? A moderate deficit and enough protein? Enough weekly sets? Recent deload? Only then change the exercise.
blocks.caption: Diagnosing a plateau

blocks.markdown:
## Check in this order

1. **Effort:** are the sets really 1–3 reps from failure? Test one set to failure on a safe exercise.
2. **Sleep and stress:** short sleep slows recovery (Module 9).
3. **Food:** a large deficit stalls muscle gain; protein matters (Modules 1 and 9).
4. **Volume:** are there enough weekly sets for that muscle?
5. **Fatigue:** when was the last deload?
6. **Programme:** only now change the exercise or the rep range.

## Plateaus in a deficit

While losing fat, holding strength steady can itself be a win. Expect slower progress in a deficit, and judge it against your waist and photos as well as the log.
**What this means for your training:** when a lift stalls for 2–3 weeks, run the checklist: effort, sleep, food, volume, fatigue. Change the exercise last, not first.

cards.back: No progress on a lift for 2–3 weeks despite consistent training.
Effort → sleep and stress → food → weekly volume → fatigue/deload → only then the programme.

questions.stem: Your push-ups stalled for three weeks during a 900 kcal-a-day deficit. What's the most likely cause?
options: The large deficit is limiting progress
Push-ups stop working after a month
questions.explanation: Large deficits stall muscle gain; moderate the deficit first.

blocks.markdown:

2. **Practice** — programming conventions used in strength coaching; labelled as practice in the lesson.

## Novelty isn't progress

Changing exercises every session feels fresh, but it makes progression hard to track. A 2022 systematic review found that planned variation can help, for example training a muscle from different angles, while excessive, random variation may compromise gains. The evidence is small, so keep it simple.

blocks.alt: Two rows across three 6-week blocks: main lifts stay the same within each block and change only between blocks; accessories rotate more freely.
blocks.caption: Stable main lifts, rotating accessories

blocks.markdown:
## A simple rule

- Keep your main lifts for a whole block, about 6–12 weeks, so you can progress them.
- Rotate accessories more freely: core moves, carries, isolation work.
- Change a main lift when it stops progressing despite the checklist, when it hurts, or when your kit allows a better version.

## Change within the pattern

When you do change, swap within the same pattern: goblet squat to Bulgarian split squat, Romanian deadlift to single-leg RDL, push-up to feet-raised push-up. The Module 4 menu is your list.
**What this means for your training:** keep main lifts for 6–12 weeks and progress them; rotate accessories freely; when you change a main lift, swap within the same pattern.

cards.back: Planned variation can help; excessive, random variation may compromise gains (2022 systematic review).

cards.front: When to change a main lift
cards.back: When it stalls despite the plateau checklist, when it hurts, or when your kit allows a better version.

questions.stem: Which approach fits the evidence best?
options: A brand-new set of exercises every session
The same main lifts for a 6–12-week block, with accessories rotating
questions.explanation: Stable main lifts let you progress; accessories can rotate.
